items._ogDesc: Stocks fell in shaky trading on Wall Street Friday, but the market remains on track for a winning week.
items.body:
Stocks fell in shaky trading on Wall Street Friday, but the market remains on track for a winning week.

Major indexes have been unsteady throughout the week as AI-focused companies pushed and pulled the market. Many of those companies have big stock values with a heavier impact on the market’s gains or losses.

The S&P 500 shifted from modest moves at the opening of trading to a 0.6 per cent drop. The index still remains on track for a weekly gain of 2.3 per cent. That would mark its first weekly gain since early October and its biggest since August.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 27 points, or 0.1 per cent, as of 1:32 p.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite fell 1.1 per cent.

The market remains unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The company has been the face of the AI industry, which has been responsible for much of the gains, and big swings, on Wall Street.

Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns. Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO.

The AI industry’s influence over Wall Street was evident again Friday. More stocks within the S&P 500 were rising rather than falling, but a slump for technology stocks with a big focus on AI dragged indexes lower.

Nvidia was again among the heaviest weights and it fell 2.8 per cent. Broadcom fell 5.1 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 10 per cent. Both companies saw their shares surge earlier this week as the management shakeup at Nvidia unfolded.

Nvidia in particular has been slipping for weeks amid wider concerns about a potential slowdown for the industry. The big worry has been whether AI will produce enough profit to justify the costly investments and big stock values.

“Nvidia’s pullback serves as a reminder of the concentration risk embedded in a market where a small number of mega-cap technology stocks have driven an outsized share of returns,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

Outside of AI, Microsoft rose 0.2 per cent, despite suffering a global outage for its web services that disrupted email accounts and other applications.

Oil prices swung a day after U.S. President Donald Trump said that the U.S. didn’t “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It was mostly unchanged at US$95.81 a barrel. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.

Stocks in Europe were mixed.

Treasury yields were mixed in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which influences mortgage rates, rose to 5.14 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday.

The yield on the two-year Treasury held steady at 4.86 per cent. It closely tracks expectations for action from the U.S. Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its benchmark interest rate at its December meeting in an effort to cool stubbornly hot inflation.

A report on Friday showed that wholesale inflation cooled a bit last month, but remains very high. The report measures inflation experienced by businesses, before it can reach consumers. Inflation at the consumer level remains stubbornly high at well above three per cent. That’s also much higher than the Fed’s preferred target of two per cent.

Rising energy prices because of the U.S. war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising.

The latest wholesale inflation report also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.

“That suggests inflation is working its way into the broader economy rather than remaining concentrated in the original areas of price pressure,” said Chris Osmond, chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors, in a research note. “If that continues, it becomes much harder for the Fed to simply look through inflation as temporary.”

The central bank held rates steady at its last meeting, following a previous rate hike. The latest hot updates on inflation have prompted economists to overwhelmingly expect a rate hike at the upcoming December meeting, with another hike likely to follow in January.

Rate hikes by the Fed can cool inflation, but that makes borrowing more expensive and can slow economic growth.

AP Business Writers Chan Ho-Him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

By Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga

items.description: Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending the four-and-a-half year-old war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”

items._ogDesc: Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending the four-and-a-half year-old war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”
items.body:
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates -- Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending the four-and-a-half year-old war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”

Hopes of ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered, however, by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year.

There’s nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia’s wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians’ will as another winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country’s power grid.

Neither Rubio nor Zelenskyy attended the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The session lasted four hours and another is scheduled for a second day Wednesday.

Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv met as Washington, represented by U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, renewed its push to stop the fighting.

“It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive,” Rubio said in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, although he urged patience. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard. It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.”

Zelenskyy said the talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to comment publicly said Ukraine and Russia talked about a large scale prisoner swap, although the details will be discussed in the coming days.

The 3-way meeting was the first since February

The two-day session is the first such meeting since February on Russia’s full-scale invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

Kushner said he believed there were “some good ideas how to bridge” the differences between the two sides.

Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television Monday night that “I don’t have overly high expectations” for the talks.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Kushner says the U.S. aims to build on past experience

Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to “create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past.”

“We take what’s worked, we try to identify what’s failed, why we’re in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace,” he said.

The commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, said the U.S. delegation looked forward “to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we’ve made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace.”

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv’s delegation, thanked the U.S. for its peace efforts.

“Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine,” he said.

Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”

Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.

Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

Russia and Ukraine hold to their demands

The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO and accept strict limits on its military, among other issues.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory. He also rejects any limits on Ukraine’s military or its arrangements with western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.

Moscow and Kyiv sent experienced negotiators

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first full-fledged peace negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022, although exploratory talks took place earlier in neighboring Belarus. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

Ukraine’s delegation includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov.

The U.S. says a broader European security deal is in the works

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”

Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.”

Moscow has welcomed that approach. “The idea of defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russian-Ukrainian conflict, is quite sensible,” said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

John Leicester in Paris, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed.

Correction

This Associated Press story was updated on Nov. 13, 2026, to correct that Grynkewich was attending the talks in Abu Dhabi in his capacity as the commander of U.S. forces in Europe.

items.title: Bessent blames Lutnick’s U.S. Commerce Department for not restricting Nvidia chips to China
items.description: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the U.S. Commerce Department’s delay in implementing controls over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China.

(Leila Navidi /Minnesota Star Tribune via AP)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Leila Navidi</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the U.S. Commerce Department’s delay in implementing controls over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the U.S. Commerce Department’s delay in implementing restrictions over the export of certain Nvidia chips to China.

Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favour of adding Megaspeed to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.

“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” he said, referring to an older generation of the company’s advanced AI chips. Commerce “has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

  • Latest updates on international news here

Bessent’s comments were an unusually public rebuke of the Commerce Department, which oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods.

The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website, play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, the New York Times has reported. China has denied allegations of spying.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang.

The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia’s more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia’s chips through companies like Megaspeedd, which has purchased more than US$4 billion worth of Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors.

The split in President Donald Trump’s cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia’s computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by Open AI and Anthropic.

The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies’ lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions.

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.

Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House’s situation room.

Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected spy.

Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick’s actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill.

On Thursday, Oregan Sen. Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Rep. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Wyden and Neal are the top Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees, respectively.

Trump’s approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, said he has questions for the commerce secretary and urged him to hold a press conference to explain what he knew.

“The Commerce Department greenlit $4 billion of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr. Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why,” Kennedy said. “I want to know why the Commerce Department did it in light of the export controls, and everything I read indicates that this was a decision by the secretary himself.”

Kennedy added that Lutnick should testify before the Senate and should be subpoenaed if necessary.

Huang resigned Thursday after news that he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, according to The Times.

Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports.

On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.

Mike Catalini and Christopher Rugaber, The Associated Press

items.body:
HAMILTON -- Stelco is recalling 175 temporarily laid off workers as it plans to restart its Hamilton, Ont., finishing operations on Dec. 1.

The company says the move is due to increased customer demand.

Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. raised the ire of Ottawa when it announced the layoffs in September.

The federal government said the cuts went against conditions it set when it approved the American company’s purchase of the steelmaker.

Cleveland-Cliffs cited U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as reasons for the cuts.

However, it says it has now reached agreement with a sufficient volume of its customers to restart the operations and recall all of the laid off workers.

The company noted that it will take several weeks to restart the operations, but that all affected employees will be made whole retroactively for the standard wages they would have received during the period in which they were temporarily laid off.

items.title: Great Outdoors Comedy Festival organizer enters bankruptcy
items.description: The company that put on the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival declared bankruptcy on Friday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Set up for the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival can be seen in Kinsmen Park on July 11, 2024. (David Ewasuk/CTV News Edmonton)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The company that put on the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival declared bankruptcy on Friday.
items.body:
The company that put on the Great Outdoors Comedy Festival declared bankruptcy on Friday.

Trixstar Productions Ltd. founder and president Mike Anderson said in a public statement that the company faced “significant financial challenges, and despite our efforts to address them, we were unable to establish a financially sustainable path forward.”

On Friday, the websites for both the comedy event and Trixstar redirected to the statement, in which Anderson apologized for the uncertainty and hardship created for employees, collaborators and fans.

He directed anyone with questions about outstanding payments, creditor claims and tickets to contact insolvency and debt service MNP, which was appointed the licensed insolvency trustee of Trixstar’s estate.

Comedy fans in Edmonton have been awaiting refunds for a July show that was cancelled due to weather, as well as in Mississauga, whose September show was abruptly and indefinitely postponed.

MNP has set up a contact page and is expected to contact all known creditors within a business week.

“No determination has been made regarding future Great Outdoors Comedy Festival events. We are hopeful that, through this process, there may be an opportunity for the festival to find a new home and continue in some form,” Anderson said.

The Great Outdoors Comedy Festival was created in 2021.

items.body:
Jason Del Vicario, Portfolio Manager, Hillside Wealth Management, iA Private Wealth

Focus: North American & Global Stocks

Top Picks: PR Times, Mortgage Advice Bureau, Dunelm

Our thoughts never waver regardless of the macro backdrop; if anything, we favour challenging economic periods as these are the times when high-quality businesses are available at favourable prices. In our opinion, the primary two factors that determine the quality of a company are: operators have strong shareholdings in the company and the company has a demonstrated history of consistently generating strong returns on invested capital. We run a concentrated portfolio of 32 global businesses that meet our strict quality criteria.

Our top 10 positions represent 62 per cent of our equity weighting. We view multiple currency exposure as a strength (no hedging). We think and behave with a long-term mindset. When one’s investment time frame is decades and not months or weeks, short term factors beyond our control such as interest rates, inflation and geopolitics become irrelevant, as we assume we’ll encounter all sorts of macro regimes over time.

We own a collection of businesses that we feel can compound shareholder wealth strongly over decades. We also wish to note that we will only ever feature companies that we own.

In addition, our top picks will always be those that we own that we feel offer the most compelling value at the time.

  • Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters

PR Times (3922 Tokyo)

PR Times runs Japan’s dominant press-release distribution platform — 133,784 client companies, up 14 per cent year on year, and two-thirds of all listed Japanese companies use it. It is a network business: the more companies that publish on it, the more indispensable it becomes to journalists, and the harder it is to displace. The ownership is aligned with us: founder Takumi Yamaguchi, who still runs the company as president and CEO, owns 6.7 per cent of the stock, and management as a whole holds about eight per cent — real skin in the game. Its parent, Vector, holds the majority stake, but the people running the business are owners alongside us.

On returns on capital it clears our bar comfortably — return on equity has averaged about 20 per cent over the last four years and reached 26 per cent last year, with return on capital employed around 34 per cent. The shares are down 19 per cent this year after a soft first half, and the market has priced the disappointment while missing the capital-allocation change announced with the results — the dividend-on-equity standard lifted from two to nine per cent, with the fiscal 2027 dividend forecast at ¥74.30 a share against ¥13.80 last year.

At ¥2,244 the stock trades at about 13.5 times trailing earnings. We started the position in early August at ¥2,030 and added through the autumn, most recently in late October at ¥2,247–2,301.

Mortgage Advice Bureau (MAB LON)

Mortgage Advice Bureau is the U.K.’s largest mortgage intermediary, with about 8.2 per cent of new U.K. mortgage lending and more than 2,100 advisers — a toll on every purchase, remortgage and product transfer that passes through its network.

The ownership is what we look for: founder Peter Brodnicki still runs the company and owns about 18 per cent of it, with insiders holding nearly a quarter of the shares between them. Returns on capital are solid rather than spectacular — return on equity has averaged about 26 per cent over five years and about 20 per cent more recently, with return on invested capital in the mid-teens — and the business grew revenue 20 per cent last year while taking share in a flat market.

The shares are down 42 per cent this year, and the reason is cost, not demand: completions rose 16 per cent in the first half while administrative expenses rose 22 per cent, and management cut full-year profit guidance in September.

The price now assumes the cost problem is permanent; we think it is fixable, and the founder’s 18 per cent says he thinks so too.

At 400.5p the stock trades at about 9 times trailing adjusted earnings. We started the position on October 13 at 342p, just above the 52-week low, and added through that week at 365–376p.

Dunelm is the U.K.’s leading homewares retailer, with 7.9 per cent of the combined homewares and furniture market, and it is the rare retailer that has kept growing share in a soft market. This is the textbook case on both of our tests. The founding Adderley family still owns about 38 per cent of the company, with Will Adderley as deputy chairman — the family governs, and professional management runs the shops.

Returns on capital are exceptional and, more importantly, sustained: return on capital employed has averaged about 48 per cent over five years and return on invested capital about 31 per cent, with not a single weak year in the run. The stock is down 21 per cent this year, which is the opportunity: at 896.5p it trades at 11.7 times last year’s earnings, and it pays an ordinary dividend of 45.5p — about 5.1 per cent — plus a 25p special dividend, with the final 28.5p paid November 17.

Net debt is £95 million against £155 million of free cash flow, so the payout is well covered. We own the market leader in a fragmented category, run by its founding family, earning 30 per cent-plus on invested capital, at under 12 times earnings.

We started the position on September 23 at 788p and added on September 24 and October 2 at about 784p.

items._ogDesc: Saudi Arabia’s The Helicopter Company has finalized an order for 12 Bombardier business jets worth about US$568 million, the Canadian planemaker said on Friday, as the Public Investment Fund-backed operator expands into fixed-wing aviation.
items.body:
Saudi Arabia’s The Helicopter Company has finalized an order for 12 Bombardier business jets worth about US$568 million, the Canadian planemaker said on Friday, as the Public Investment Fund-backed operator expands into fixed-wing aviation.

The firm order covers five Challenger 3500 jets, five Global 5500 jets and two Global 8000 jets, Bombardier said, with THC retaining options for an additional 48 aircraft.

Largely known for its helicopter-charter operations, THC announced plans to move into fixed-wing business aviation at the Farnborough airshow earlier this year, pushing to broaden its offerings as demand for private-jet travel rises.

THC had signed a letter of intent with Bombardier for up to 60 aircraft at the airshow.

As part of the partnership with THC, Bombardier said it has committed to a long-term strategic investment that includes a local footprint in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The Helicopter Company also signed a deal last November with electric air taxi firm Archer Aviation to develop, test and potentially deploy electric aircraft in the Kingdom.

(Reporting by Nandan Mandayam and Shivansh Tiwary in Bengaluru; Editing by Jonathan Ananda)

items.title: Ottawa, province hope 'aggressive package' can prevent Stellantis plant sale: Joly
items.description: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she’s still hopeful she can prevent the company from selling its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to Roshel.
items._ogDesc: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she’s still hopeful she can prevent the company from selling its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to Roshel.
items.body:
TORONTO — A day after threatening to sue Stellantis to recoup federal cash given to the automaker, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she’s still hopeful she can prevent the company from selling its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to Roshel.

Joly says Ottawa has “put an aggressive package to Stellantis to prevent the sale and we are still in solution mode to prevent the sale.”

She says she also plans to present “new scenarios” during an upcoming meeting with the company’s global CEO Antonio Filosa.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The minister made those comments during an announcement Friday in Vaughan, Ont., alongside Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli, who says there are supports available to Stellantis if it can “buy some time” rather than moving forward with the sale to the defence contractor.

Joly reiterated that if Stellantis does continue down that road, it would be on the hook for “hundreds of millions of dollars” given by Ottawa so the company could retool its Brampton and Windsor facilities to produce electrified vehicles.

However, Stellantis said Thursday it intends to only repay $24 million in federal government support received for the Brampton facility’s retooling plan.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: How the Microsoft chaos impacted Canada’s mortgage industry
items.description: Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread
items.content: <p>Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639301912201989264.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Brokers report varying levels of disruption as Microsoft 365 outage spread
items.body:
Microsoft appears to finally be getting to grips with the issues that caused huge global outages in its Microsoft 365 services on Thursday and Friday, but that chaos led to its fair share of disruption across the world – and the mortgage industry.

Brokers were forced to find workarounds as email disruptions delayed closings and left lenders and lawyers unable to receive documents, raising questions about whether various industries were fully prepared for such a crisis.

David Clarke, a Nova Scotia-based mortgage broker, told Canadian Mortgage Professional his exposure was limited because he operates a personal Gmail account alongside a Microsoft-based email system, but the outage still required him to pick up the phone and clarify things with industry counterparts.

“I had a lender where I was sending stuff and they weren’t getting it,” he said. “But I was aware of the outage, so I called and we navigated it. It’s kind of weird – it was like some things got through and some things didn’t.”

Clarke said he first noticed something was up yesterday when a lawyer requested identification documents for a refinance, but never received them. In that case the delay had no consequences, but he noted how quickly the outcome could change for a purchase closing with a hard deadline.

Another problem: many professionals might not have realized they were missing anything at all. “It’s a pretty big deal,” Clarke said. “Even people that knew about the outage, they wouldn’t know that someone was trying to send them something. So it’s hard to even react to it.”

Brokers find workarounds as challenges persist

Other brokers using Gmail also saw minimal disruption, although they had to manoeuvre challenges with clients or industry partners whose platforms were affected.

Paul Meredith, principal broker and president at PMT Mortgage Corp. in Toronto, told CMP he noticed a marked drop in incoming emails even though his team is on Gmail. “We’ve been following up with clients and anything of importance by phone and text,” he said. “We’ll always do everything we can to work around life’s unexpected challenges.”

His primary concern is with enquiries that arrive during the blackout period. “I think the biggest issue here would be if there are any new inquiries trying to email us,” he said. “But they would certainly be aware of the outage so would generally call, text, or wait it out.”

For some brokers, the outage had zero effect on day-to-day operations. “Honestly, this did not impact us at all,” Taz Zaide of 6ix Mortgage Group said. “Everything moved along as usual just like any other day on our end.”

Outage compounds mortgage industry’s staffing problems

One factor that extends well beyond any single outage, Clarke said, is an industry already running short on staff. “Every [part of the] industry is so understaffed,” he said. “Everyone’s busy. So for you to even notice that you didn’t get something, you’ve got to be pretty proactive on a file to check in.”

Most professionals are reacting to emails, he said, rather than monitoring for their absence. “If I was on the road yesterday, I would have probably missed things,” he said.

The disruption extended across the mortgage industry globally. The impact was immediate and widespread for Katherine Stagg, founder and managing director of Stagg Mortgage Services in the United Kingdom.

“I didn’t actually realize how much I relied on it until it doesn’t work,” she told Mortgage Introducer. “Everything is based on your calendar, your emails, your Copilot – everything you can’t do.”

At the time of writing, Microsoft appearsto be making progress in restoring access to its platforms, although that “broad recovery” is still not complete.

Clarke said the lesson for the mortgage industry is a deeper one than technical fixes. “Things like this happen and you’ve got to be nice to people while they happen,” he said.

items.title: Here’s where RBC sees Canadian inflation landing next week
items.description: RBC forecasts October CPI will ease, setting the stage for December’s Bank of Canada rate call
items.content: <p>RBC forecasts October CPI will ease, setting the stage for December’s Bank of Canada rate call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/077/0311_638356334562976666.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: RBC forecasts October CPI will ease, setting the stage for December’s Bank of Canada rate call
items.body:
Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) economists are forecasting a slight dip in Canadian inflation for October, with the upcoming data release positioned as the final major read on consumer prices ahead of the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) December interest rate decision.

In a research note, Claire Fan, Senior Economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, and Abbey Xu, Economist at Royal Bank of Canada, project headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) growth to ease modestly to 3% year-over-year, down from 3.1% in September.

Energy prices held largely flat between September and October but remained well above year-ago levels.

Food inflation, which has cooled to near 2%, is expected to have shifted little over the same period.

Read more: Bank of Canada weighed two paths before raising rates to 2.5%

Core price pressures show signs of easing

Stripping out food and energy, RBC expects core CPI to tick down from 2.1% to 1.9% in October.

The BoC’s two preferred measures — CPI-trim and CPI-median — are forecast to hold at the same year-over-year rate after a benign 0.2% monthly gain.

On the breadth of inflation, the report noted that the diffusion index used by RBC to track the share of consumer basket items seeing abnormally high inflation “is expected to have remained relatively narrow, pointing to limited spillover from energy to other components of consumer prices outside inter-city transport.”

Even so, the economists cautioned that “limited evidence to date does not rule out the potential for more significant spillover in the future.”

Read more: What Canada's latest inflation reading means for mortgages

The case for a December hike — and the doubts

RBC’s base case remains a December rate hike to bring the overnight rate to 2.75%, the midpoint of the BoC’s estimated neutral range.

Yet the report was candid about uncertainty. “The case for a December hike is not a slam dunk,” Fan and Xu wrote, adding that “economic data since their last meeting has mostly turned softer.”

The analysts noted that “domestic gasoline prices have fallen significantly in November, back closer to levels in March as oil prices and refining margins both normalize” — removing one source of near-term upward pressure.

Despite that, the report warned that producer-level data “has pointed to a significant widening in scope, which will likely continue to trickle through supply chains before showing up in consumer prices with a lag.”

RBC’s bottom line: “Our base case remains a low conviction hike in December.”

items.title: BC foreign buyer tax wins at the Supreme Court of Canada
items.description: Canada’s highest court upholds additional property transfer tax on a jointly owned condo
items.content: <p>Canada’s highest court upholds additional property transfer tax on a jointly owned condo</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639301878525027166.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s highest court upholds additional property transfer tax on a jointly owned condo
items.body:
The Supreme Court of Canada has declined to hear a challenge to British Columbia’s additional property transfer tax (ATT), closing the final legal avenue for a Richmond couple who argued the foreign buyer levy was wrongly applied to their jointly owned condominium.

The court’s refusal, issued in November, ends a multi-year legal dispute over the gap between registered title and actual financial contribution — a distinction with direct consequences for mortgage brokers advising mixed-nationality buyers across British Columbia.

Registered title vs. actual contribution: where the tax applied

Chia-Wen Hsia, a Canadian citizen, and her partner Li-Yuan Chuang, a foreign national, signed a presale contract in 2014 for a Richmond, BC condominium declared at $474,500.

Hsia was registered as the 95% owner, while Chuang held just 5% — despite having contributed 40% of the purchase price.

Hsia explained in appellate proceedings that the arrangement reflected a cultural practice: “It is customary in Chinese culture to pay for ‘bride price’ as in the husband buying a house for the wife.”

She added: “In my husband’s case, he is not rich so he could only pay for part of the purchase price.”

The couple initially remitted ATT — levied at 20% under British Columbia’s Property Transfer Tax Act — on Chuang’s registered 5% interest only.

A subsequent BC Finance Ministry audit determined the tax was payable on the property’s full market value.

A ministry analyst assessed the additional amount owed at just over $126,000.

The property’s most recent assessed value stands at $820,000, well above the $474,500 declared at purchase.

Joel Fox of Ownright says allowing foreign buyers to purchase newly built homes could support new construction and housing supply, while continued restrictions on resale properties help address concerns around speculation. https://t.co/mkrwdSPIxq — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

A three-judge BC Court of Appeal panel ruled on January 14 in Chuang v. British Columbia (2026 BCCA 10) that the liability could have been avoided had the couple registered ownership proportionate to their financial contributions.

The province maintained the rule was designed to “prevent tax avoidance by foreign investors who own beneficial interests held indirectly by others.”

The BC Supreme Court had dismissed the initial challenge in 2024.

What the ruling means for mortgage brokers

Their lawyer, Massao Morinaga, confirmed the SCC refusal left no further legal recourse.

“It’s the end of the road judicially,” he said, noting the ATT legislation remains drafted in a way that “captures situations that are inequitable.”

The decision reinforces a fixed principle in BC tax law that registered title determines ATT exposure, not actual financial contribution.

As Brendon Ogmundson, chief economist at the BC Real Estate Association (BCREA) in Vancouver, warned in CMP’s coverage of BC’s 2026 housing tax increases, taxing the housing sector in an already weak market “will ultimately prove to be self-defeating.”

In June, BCREA formally called on the province to reform the ATT for foreign buyers as part of its pre-budget submission to the BC Select Standing Committee on Finance and Government Services.

For brokers guiding clients on mixed-nationality purchases in BC’s designated regions — an issue CMP examined in its analysis of whether Canada’s foreign homebuyer ban should be extended — the precedent is unambiguous.

With Canada’s federal foreign buyer ban now heading toward a 2029 deadline and provincial ATT rules unchanged, ensuring ownership registration reflects actual financial contribution is not merely legal housekeeping — it is the difference between a proportionate tax bill and one calculated on the property’s full market value.

items.title: Why Real Property Solutions is backing the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards
items.description: Company reaffirms its dedication to the broker community as the CMAs’ landmark 20th anniversary approaches
items.content: <p>Company reaffirms its dedication to the broker community as the CMAs’ landmark 20th anniversary approaches</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639301096509195123.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Company reaffirms its dedication to the broker community as the CMAs’ landmark 20th anniversary approaches
items.body:
As the Canadian Mortgage Awards prepare to mark their 20th anniversary on November 25, Real Property Solutions (RPS) is using its sponsorship to signal a message about the value of relationships in the mortgage industry.

The company is sponsoring the Brokerage/Team of the Year (25 Employees or More) award at the CMAs at Rebel Toronto, and head of broker channel Rishi Vaswani told Canadian Mortgage Professional the decision to back the awards reflects how it views its place in the mortgage sector.

“At RPS, we believe supporting mortgage brokers goes beyond providing reliable appraisal services,” he said. “It’s about building strong partnerships that help brokers better serve their clients and grow their businesses.”

The ceremony is one of the mortgage industry’s most prominent annual gatherings, drawing brokers, lenders and executives from across the country to showcase the best and brightest performers throughout the sector.

Vaswani said recognition counts for more than merely its ceremonial value. In a turbulent borrowing environment marked by rising interest rates, affordability challenges and economic unease, the crucial part played by mortgage brokers is coming into even sharper focus than usual.

“Mortgage brokers play an important role in helping Canadians navigate some of their biggest financial decisions,” he said. “Behind every successful brokerage is a team committed to earning clients’ trust, delivering great service and adapting to an evolving market.”

He sees industry recognition as a way to lift standards across the board and ensure that Canadians continue to receive top-notch service from the mortgage community.

“Recognizing excellence celebrates those achievements while setting a benchmark for the broader industry,” he said. “It’s also an opportunity to share what great looks like, and inspire others to continue raising the bar.”

What’s new with RPS

RPS, which delivers appraisal management, automated valuations and housing intelligence for the Canadian mortgage industry, has prioritized expanding its offerings for brokers beyond core appraisal management this year, according to Vaswani.

As well as the new Track My Order feature and continued development of the House Price Tracker and Appraisal Overview Report, broker education has been a key focus. RPS has expanded its offering of accredited webinars and practical resources, aiming to help brokers navigate appraisal challenges and handle client conversations with confidence.

“As the go-to appraisal partner for brokers, we’re committed to continually finding new ways to make their work easier, strengthen their client relationships, and support their business growth,” Vaswani said.

With 2027 just around the corner, mortgage borrowers are likely to continue navigating a choppy environment for the foreseeable future, marked by a flood of mortgage renewals at higher rates.

Vaswani said the opportunity for service providers in that environment is clear.

“Looking ahead to 2027, we believe brokers will increasingly benefit from partners who can simplify processes, provide reliable property intelligence and help them build lasting client relationships,” he said.

As the awards draw nearer, Vaswani noted how RPS views itself and the value it provides within the industry. “We are more than an appraisal management company,” he said. “We’re the go-to appraisal partner for brokers providing reliable valuation services, greater transparency throughout the appraisal process and practical tools that help them strengthen client relationships and grow their businesses.”

Gearing up for a big night on November 25

The CMAs’ two-decade milestone marks a significant moment for an awards ceremony that’s celebrated the industry over a dramatic 20-year span.

Those have been some of the most eventful years in the industry’s history, spanning financial crisis in the late 2000s, tightening mortgage qualification guidelines in the 2010s, and the unprecedented housing market boom – followed by a spell of sharply climbing rates – of the 2020s.

Against that backdrop, Vaswani said the Excellence Awardees – nominees for each prize, who will battle it out to be named overall winners on November 25 – reflect the professionalism and dedication that continue to shine across the mortgage sector.

“Their achievements are a testament to the talent and commitment across our industry,” he said.

items.title: Bank of Canada weighed two paths before raising rates to 2.5%
items.description: Minutes show Governing Council accepted the risk of acting, fearing entrenched inflation more than higher rates
items.content: <p>Minutes show Governing Council accepted the risk of acting, fearing entrenched inflation more than higher rates</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639301086688518718.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Minutes show Governing Council accepted the risk of acting, fearing entrenched inflation more than higher rates
items.body:
The Bank of Canada’s Governing Council moved forward with its first interest rate increase since July 2023 despite deep uncertainty about global energy markets and Canada-US trade relations, according to deliberation minutes of the bank’s October 28 policy meeting.

The minutes covered discussions between October 20 and October 28 among Governor Tiff Macklem, Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers and four deputy governors.

The council considered two options — holding the policy rate at 2.25% or lifting it to 2.5% — before concluding the balance of risk had tilted toward action.

“They recognized that uncertainty did not mean inaction, but they agreed they would need to proceed carefully to assess how economic developments would affect their outlook,” the minutes stated.

Canada’s labour market shed 4,700 jobs in October, pushing the national unemployment rate to 6.7% from 6.5%, a third consecutive month of deterioration that is now complicating the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) path to a December rate hike. https://t.co/M8Ce4IYrjH — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

Energy shock sharpens the inflation outlook

An eight-month-old conflict in the Middle East had pushed the benchmark price of crude oil approximately US$35 higher per barrel than assumed in the Bank’s July Monetary Policy Report. The minutes show this was the dominant pressure point in Governing Council’s deliberations.

“With the war in its eighth month and no resolution on the horizon, members exchanged views on whether a higher policy interest rate was needed to mitigate the risk that higher energy costs would spread to other goods and services,” the minutes stated.

Canada’s annual inflation rate reached 3.2% in September, according to Statistics Canada, driven almost entirely by higher energy and transportation costs.

Core inflation remained near 2%, but council members warned the buffer was narrowing.

“Cost pressures were building and would eventually be reflected in core measures as these costs make their way into consumer prices,” the minutes stated, adding that even without further pass-through, “the energy shock alone would keep CPI inflation at around 3% for more than a year.”

Governing Council was also direct about the limits of its tools.

“Members agreed that while monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, it can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation,” the minutes stated.

The Bank’s revised projections now see headline CPI inflation reaching 3.5% by year-end 2026 and remaining above 3% through most of 2027, before returning to the 2% target by mid-2028.

Brokers push back on the bank’s reasoning

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, said the decision extends an already prolonged housing correction.

“A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don’t see things turning until there’s a rate drop,” Fox previously said.

Jessica Rickerby, president of the Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) in Toronto, challenged the bank’s underlying logic.

“While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is — at present — a hypothetical,” Rickerby said.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Vancouver, said the Bank was drawing an explicit parallel to its pandemic-era policy missteps.

“The communications make it clear that the central bank wants to stay ahead of the curve and ‘avoid the debacle’ of 2022-23, when it was too late to raise the policy rate,” she wrote.

The Bank of Canada’s next rate decision is scheduled for December 9.

items.content: <p>FCT stalwart adds chief executive title at Canada’s title insurance provider</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639301069149411183.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: FCT stalwart adds chief executive title at Canada’s title insurance provider
items.body:
Title insurance and real estate technology provider FCT has named Daniela DeTommaso as president and chief executive officer, effective January 1, 2027.

DeTommaso, who has led the Oakville, Ontario-based company as president since June 2021, will assume the dual role. 

Michael LeBlanc, FCT’s current chief executive, shifts his focus to president of the international division at parent company First American Financial Corporation, based in Santa Ana, California.

The appointment marks more than 30 years at FCT for DeTommaso, who began her career in the company’s legal department before rising through increasingly senior roles across the organization.

From legal counsel to chief executive

DeTommaso’s trajectory reflects an unusually deep institutional knowledge. By the late 2000s, she was leading FCT’s residential lending solutions group, overseeing its mortgage-facing product lines.

She later guided FCT’s data and innovation strategy before being elevated to president in 2021 to oversee all product, operations, sales, and marketing functions. She holds an LL.B. and serves as vice-chair of Hospice Vaughan in Ontario.

Earlier this year, she joined the judging panel for CMP’s 2026 Top 50 Women of Influence, a recognition in which FCT has long been an active participant. 

“Daniela is an exceptional leader whose strategic vision, sound judgment and commitment to our customers and people have made a lasting impact on FCT,” LeBlanc said.

“Having worked alongside Daniela for nearly three decades, I have seen firsthand her ability to bring people together, navigate change and translate strategy into meaningful results. I have tremendous confidence in her ability to lead FCT forward.”

DeTommaso acknowledged both the responsibility and the continuity ahead.

“FCT’s strength comes from our people, customer-focused culture and commitment to continually evolve,” she said.

“I look forward to working with our talented teams to build on that foundation, further strengthen our business and deliver solutions that create lasting value for our customers and partners.”

An appointment that matters beyond FCT

Her elevation to chief executive carries significance across the broader Canadian mortgage sector. According to CMP’s 2026 roundtable of Canadian mortgage finance leaders, women hold just 4% of CEO roles in the Canadian mortgage industry. 

As chief executive, DeTommaso will bear responsibility for strategy, people, customer relationships, operational discipline, and capital allocation.

LeBlanc will continue to oversee FCT as part of his international remit, to whom DeTommaso will report.

Founded in 1991 and headquartered in Oakville, Ontario, FCT is a wholly owned subsidiary of First American Financial Corporation.

The company employs more than 1,200 professionals across Canada and serves approximately 450 lenders, 43,000 legal professionals, and 5,000 recovery experts, as well as mortgage brokers, real estate agents, and builders nationwide.

Its product suite covers residential and commercial title insurance, property intelligence, default solutions, and digital real estate transaction technology across the full property lifecycle.

items._ogDesc: Greater Toronto’s purpose-built rental vacancy hits 13.3% as completions reach a record, with another 34,545 units under construction.
items.body:
The Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area (GTHA) rental market is tightening—if you exclude new supply. A new report from Urbanation shows a falling vacancy rate for stabilized purpose-built rental buildings in Q3. However, including new buildings still trying to find their first tenants reveals roughly 1 in 8 units are vacant, with a lot more in the pipeline.

Greater Toronto Rental Vacancy Reaches 13.3% Including New Buildings

When we reported on Q1 back in May, nearly 1 in 19 apartments sat vacant in Greater Toronto’s stabilized rental buildings completed since 2000. That’s now dropped to 1 in 33, with the vacancy rate falling from 5.4% to 3.0% in Q3. The catch here is the term stabilized, which Urbanation defines as having reached 95% occupancy.

Stabilized is an industry term used to assess buildings that have moved beyond their initial leasing phase and established an operating income. However, focusing on those buildings excludes newer projects still struggling to attract tenants—even though those vacant apartments compete for the same renters.

A more comprehensive look tells a very different story. The rental vacancy rate jumps to 13.3% in Q3 when including buildings in the “lease up” phase to hit that 95% goal, up from 12.1% last year. The 1 in 33 vacant units looks more like over 1 in 8 when those are included.

New Rental Apartments Arrive Faster Than Tenants Fill Them

The number of occupied purpose-built rental apartments rose by 1,911 units in Q3. Builders completed a record 2,704 apartments over the same three months, exceeding the growth in occupied units by 793. Even during the busiest leasing quarter of the year, new supply outpaced demand.

That gap comes despite record growth in occupied apartments. Through September, the number rose by 5,092 units, up 22% from the same period last year.

Rents after incentives remained 1.5% below a year earlier in purpose-built rental buildings surveyed in both periods. Landlords also pulled back on incentives: 60% of projects offered them, down from 67% in Q2, while one month of free rent replaced two months as the most common offer. Headline incentives shrank, but rents remain lower than last year even after accounting for fewer incentives.

Greater Toronto Has 34,500 Purpose-Built Rentals Under Construction

Even as the overall purpose-built vacancy rises, a lot more supply is on the way. Builders started 12,106 purpose-built rental units through September, up 82% from the same period last year and already exceeding the full-year total for 2025. That brought the number of units under construction to 34,545. Purpose-built rentals now account for nearly half of all apartments under construction in the GTHA.

Urbanation expects the drop in condo completions to outweigh the rise in purpose-built rental units. The shift isn’t an accident, as it follows policymakers’ push to use taxpayer-backed incentives to grow institutional investment in the sector.

items.title: Canadian building permits slide as multi-unit plans retreat
items.description: Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally
items.content: <p>Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639300980349360319.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Building permits fell in September as multi-family construction plans retreated nationally
items.body:
The total value of building permits issued across Canada fell 4.1% to $12.9 billion in September, Statistics Canada reported Thursday. A sharp pullback in multi-family residential intentions signalled continued strain on new housing supply.

On a constant dollar basis (2023=100), permit values declined 4.5% from August but remained 1.9% above the same month a year earlier.

Building permits, surveyed across approximately 2,400 municipalities representing 95% of the country’s population, are a leading indicator of construction activity, though issuance does not guarantee that construction will proceed.

Multi-family weakness dominates the residential slide

Residential building permit values fell 5.8% to $7.8 billion in September. The multi-family component drove the decline, sliding $529.3 million to $5.1 billion.

British Columbia (-$292.1 million) and Alberta (-$186.8 million) recorded the steepest retreats, with eight provinces and one territory contributing to the drop.

Year-to-date, residential permit values have fallen 5.2% in 2026, according to Statistics Canada.

Single-family permits moved in the opposite direction, rising $53.6 million to $2.7 billion, largely on strength from Ontario (+$103.3 million).

Non-residential intentions edged down $77.1 million to $5.1 billion, as a decline in institutional construction (-$171.5 million) was partially offset by industrial permit growth (+$90.9 million), driven by Ontario and Nova Scotia.

What September’s data signals for the construction pipeline

The September result caps a weak third quarter. Total building permit values fell $1.5 billion to $38.8 billion in Q3, a 3.6% quarterly drop, with non-residential permits recording their sharpest quarterly decline since Q2 2020.

Nationally, 71,300 homes were authorized for construction in Q3, down from 78,500 in the same period of 2025. That's a year-over-year decline of roughly 9.2%.

For mortgage brokers navigating this constrained supply environment, managing client expectations around future inventory has become central to daily practice.

Major banks and homebuilders are pressing Ottawa to act, having urged the federal government to ease mortgage qualification rules for first-time buyers of newly built homes in a 29-point reform plan released this week.

“Building permits provide an early signal of future residential construction activity, while housing starts capture construction that has begun and offer the best indication of future housing supply,” Mathieu Laberge, chief economist and senior vice-president of Housing Insights at Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), previously said.

“Together, these measures show how development intentions translate into real construction activity, providing a more complete picture of the residential construction market’s trajectory.”

Kevin Hughes, CMHC’s deputy chief economist, reinforced that view: “Building permit data provides additional context for this pattern, pointing to a construction pipeline that remains subdued, in line with CMHC’s Housing Market Outlook.”

Mike Kazarian, a mortgage broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages in Toronto, Ontario, explained how the condo segment faces a prolonged recovery. 

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad. It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales,” he recently told CMP. 

Separately, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation data for September showed housing starts at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate (SAAR) of 248,896 units. That's roughly 3% above August’s figure, with the CMHC six-month moving average edging up 0.6% to 250,411 units.

 The B.C.
items._ogDesc: VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year. The B.C.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — British Columbia recorded 5,670 home sales last month, a drop of almost 11 per cent from October last year.

The B.C. Real Estate Association says in a statement that the average sale price of a home in the province this October fell about 2.8 per cent from about $977,000 last year to just short of $950,000.

The latest numbers come after the association released its fourth quarter forecast this week, projecting that B.C. home sales would slide 4.5 per cent this year from 2025 to about 67,000 units.

Association chief economist Brendon Ogmundson cites mounting market challenges from interest rates, slower immigration, oil-price shock and U.S. trade tensions, potentially contributing to the decline in the latest monthly numbers.

Ogmundson says more-affordable areas of the province have been resilient, with Kamloops seeing a 12 per cent rise in home sales last month.

But he says Metro Vancouver and the rest of the Lower Mainland continue to be hampered by "global headwinds and hawkish monetary policy," with Greater Vancouver sales falling 10 per cent to just over 2,000 units sold in October.

“Recoveries in more-expensive regions of the province are dependent on a retracing of rates and oil prices such that prospective buyers regain confidence after several volatile quarters,” Ogmundson says in the statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: Entre Nous Femmes Proposes 2-Tower Affordable Rental Project In Surrey
items.description:
Vancouver-based not-for-profit Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society is planning a new project that would add around 750 mixed-income affordable rental units to the City of Surrey, according to a new rezoning application.

Entre Nous Femmes, which is French for “Amongst us, Women,” describes itself as “one of Canada’s first women-led community housing organizations” and their mission focuses on “the unique needs of women, gender-diverse groups, single-parent families, seniors, people with disabilities, and other equity-deserving groups,” according to their website, which adds that they currently have a portfolio of 15 properties with over 700 affordable rental homes.

The site of the new Surrey project is 9883 140 Street, located about midway between 100 Avenue and the Fraser Highway, a few blocks east of the Expo Line SkyTrain’s King George Station. The site is currently occupied by an affordable housing community called Jessica Place.

According to their rezoning application, Jessica Place is currently home to 40 below-market rental townhouses, but the homes are “approaching its end of life.” The new proposal is intended to replace those units, with current residents to have the opportunity to move into the new buildings, while adding new supply.

9883 140 Street and the proposed road dedications. (WW+P Architects, Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society)

The application seeks to subdivide the site into two parcels and rezone the site to allow for one 35-storey tower and one 39-storey tower that would together deliver 748 affordable rental units. The proposal would require the Official Community Plan (OCP) designation for the site to be amended from Mid-Rise I to High-Rise I.

Phase One would be located at the centre of the site (Block 1 in the image above) and be home to the 35-storey tower, which will include 327 units. The proposed suite mix consists of 39 studio units, 147 one-bedroom units, 80 two-bedroom units, 50 three-bedroom units, and 11 four-bedroom units. The building would include 99 vehicle parking spaces, as well as some office space for the property management team.

Phase Two would then be located towards the west (Block 2) and be home to the 39-storey tower, which will include 421 units. The proposed suite mix is 42 studio units, 211 one-bedroom units, 84 two-bedroom units, 63 three-bedroom units, and 21 four-bedroom units. This building would include 167 vehicle parking spaces.

There is no Phase Three, but a small piece of the site in the northeast corner (Block 3) is intended to be consolidated with the property to the south — 9568 140 Street, a condo building — in the future. It will be used as a community garden in the interim.

The site plan for the 9883 140 Street proposal. (WW+P Architects, Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society)

According to a City planning report, Entre Nous Femmes has committed to providing all 748 units as mixed-income affordable rental units (rent-geared-to-income or low-end-of-market), but the precise affordability levels of the units are still being finalized, although a minimum of 40 units will be provided at below-market rents, replacing the existing units as required under City policy.

Amenities across the two buildings include meeting rooms, playrooms, a gymnasium, town hall room, multi-purpose rooms, co-working space, outdoor patios, playgrounds, and potentially a basketball court at the northwest corner of the site.

“The proposed development does not comply with the existing land use designation in the Official Community Plan but it does support policies in relation to increasing housing diversity and supply in areas with good access to transit and other amenities,” said City staff.

“The proposed development features high-quality architecture, appropriate site planning and an improved streetscape which benefits the overall surrounding neighbourhood. Staff support the development proposal on the subject site given that it will provide much needed mixed-income affordable rental housing within City Centre and supports the goal of achieving higher density development within close proximity to frequent transit corridors.”

One of the towers proposed for 9883 140 Street. (Entres Nous Femmes Housing Society)

On its project website, Entre Nous Femmes says all of the existing residents will gradually need to relocate temporarily as the new development will require the demolition of all the existing buildings on site. Tenants were made aware of the redevelopment plans as early as January 2025.

According to a July 2025 bulletin, the plan was to have all residents relocated by February 2027, construction commence in Summer 2027, and occupancy take place in Summer 2030, but that timeline entailed the rezoning application be approved in Summer 2026, which did not occur, so the timeline has now likely changed.

Entre Nous Femmes has submitted a rezoning application for the overall project plus a general and detailed development permit for Phase One. Earlier this week, during the first meeting of Surrey City Council following last month’s municipal elections, the associated bylaws were granted first and second readings without discussion then advanced to a public hearing scheduled for Monday, November 23.

items.title: Banks, builders urge Ottawa to ease stress test for new-home buyers
items.description: Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing
items.content: <p>Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639300957594987414.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Coalition’s 29-point housing plan targets down payments, foreign buyers and condo financing
items.body:
Canada’s five largest banks and a group of major homebuilders want Ottawa to loosen the mortgage stress test for first-time buyers of newly built homes.

The proposal is one of 29 recommendations in a report released this week to inform the federal review of the National Housing Strategy.

The National Housing and Investment Initiative (NHII) pairs executives from Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Royal Bank of Canada, Scotiabank and Toronto-Dominion Bank with developers including Mattamy Homes and Minto Group.

Its central argument is that homes built for ownership will not get built unless buyers can qualify for financing.

How the stress test could change for first-time buyers

The group wants a sliding minimum qualifying rate tied to mortgage term and buyer type. It would set a softer test for first-time buyers of new construction, for example qualifying them at the contract rate plus 1.5 percentage points rather than two.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) is leaving the stress test unchanged, keeping qualification at 5.25% or two points above a borrower’s contract rate, whichever is higher, after it reviewed its mortgage stress test rules in January.

The report also calls for a federal down payment assistance program limited to new homes. 

“The current stress test is a valuable prudential tool but may be too blunt an instrument by excluding otherwise creditworthy borrowers,” the report said.

The coalition acknowledged the trade-off. “However, there are concerns that loosening the rules could, among other things, cause a spike in resale home prices and harm affordability,” the report said.

It argued that limiting relief to newly built homes would keep that pressure off the resale market.

Foreign buyer and condo asks meet a slumping new-build market

The report names five priorities:

  1. a permanent version of Ontario’s enhanced harmonized sales tax (HST) rebate
  2. a capital gains rollover, modelled on the US Section 1031 provision, for investors who reinvest proceeds in purpose-built rentals
  3. alternatives to development charges
  4. a foreign buyer ban exemption for new construction
  5. an Owner-Occupied Construction Loan Program for condominiums

Ottawa has already acted on one of them. Its 2026 budget kept the foreign buyer ban but loosened its terms to exclude newly built properties.

Joel Fox, co-founder and chief operating officer of Ownright, warned Canadian Mortgage Professional of the risk that those places just sit empty. 

Joel Fox of Ownright says allowing foreign buyers to purchase newly built homes could support new construction and housing supply, while continued restrictions on resale properties help address concerns around speculation. https://t.co/mkrwdSPIxq — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 10, 2026

The report says the HST reforms helped sell about 5,000 additional homes in the program’s first three months.

Micky Khaneka of MKG Mortgages in Toronto said Ontario’s temporary HST rebate on new homes “has sparked some renewed interest in the newer homes, especially new builds.” 

Condos remain the weak spot. According to the report, condos have historically supplied upwards of 40% of Canada’s urban housing stock, yet they have no equivalent to the $55-billion Apartment Construction Loan Program for rentals.

“I think the outlook for condos is still bad,” Mike Kazarian, a Toronto broker with Lenders’ Choice Mortgages, told CMP this week. 

“It’s going to be two or three years because the population growth has basically plummeted. If that continues, there’s a lot of inventory right now and a lot of the preconstruction builders are doing fire sales.”

Brad Carr, CEO, Canada, at Mattamy Homes and NHII co-chair, said the country’s goals “will require a significant expansion of the development pipeline, greater access to long-term capital, modernized financial regulation, predictable immigration policies and access to better data to support all of those decisions.”

items.title: Industry leaders urge new B.C. government to revisit housing policies
items.description: Real estate industry groups want tax changes, lower construction costs to revive housing development
items._ogDesc: Real estate industry groups want tax changes, lower construction costs to revive housing development
items.body:
People in B.C.’s real estate industry are urging the incoming provincial government to revisit housing policies in an effort to revive the province’s housing market.

Groups representing developers and real estate agents say the government should assess existing policies and determine which ones to modify or scrap, as well as consider introducing new measures to reduce construction costs and encourage more housing development.

“We have a cost of delivery crisis. It costs more to build than what people can afford,” said Michael Drummond, CEO of the Urban Development Institute (UDI).

Metro Vancouver’s new condo construction saw a 15-year low in the first half of 2026, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), highlighting weak presales and high construction costs.

“So effectively when the current amount of housing is sold, there is no next new project,” said Drummond. “When immigration normalizes, we're going to get another spike in prices.”

Drummond said he hopes the BC Conservatives will revisit policies introduced by the previous NDP government that could potentially add to construction costs. He said he wants the government to pause mandatory increases to the BC Energy Step Code and Zero Carbon Step Code.

The former BC Liberak introduced the BC Energy Step Code in 2017 to gradually improve energy efficiency in new buildings, and the Zero Carbon Step Code in 2023 to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from new buildings. He wants the government to pause mandatory increases to the BC Energy Step Code and Zero Carbon Step Code.

For large buildings, the province currently requires Step 2 of the Energy Step Code, meaning new construction must be about 20 per cent more energy efficient than required under the previous building standards. Higher steps require greater energy efficiency.

Drummond wants the provincial minimum for large buildings held at Step 2.

UDI is also urging the incoming Conservative government to cancel PST expansion to professional services and introduce a development charge reduction program modelled on Ontario’s recent approach.

“The previous government tried to rely on demand-side measures, they've tried to rely on taxes, and a tax never built a new home,” said Drummond.

The BC Real Estate Association (BCREA) is also asking the Conservative government to review the Step Code and home-energy policies, halt the planned PST expansion, and reconsider housing-related taxes, including the Speculation and Vacancy Tax introduced in 2018. The association argues that these measures add to the tax burden and the costs of purchasing a home.

“Over the last several years, we haven't exactly had a shortage of housing policy,” said Jasroop Gosal, the BCREA’s government relations manager.

Gosal pointed to the introduction of Bills 44 and 47, changes to development financing and the Energy Step Code, the Speculation and Vacancy tax, the home-flipping tax, the foreign buyer tax, housing targets and affordable housing programs.

“And the list goes on and on and on. So the question now is: what happens to all of that when governments change?”

BCREA is calling on the new government to establish a permanent Provincial Housing Policy Roundtable, bringing together different stakeholders from across B.C.’s real estate industry to review existing housing policies, as a first step.

How to measure success?

Industry leaders say they don’t expect the new government to solve the housing problem right away, but there are certain changes they hope to see within a year.

“One year is not very long when it comes to housing because of the development pipeline,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the BC Non-Profit Housing Association.

She said the industry wants to see more clarity about the government’s direction and the tools it is prepared to use, something she said has been missing for the last couple of years.

“If in one year the entire housing ecosystem understood with clarity the direction that the government wants to go, what tools it's prepared to use, and the level of investment it's required to make into affordability for British Columbians … that would be helpful to the whole sector,” she said.

“That provides the predictability where you then have the sector investing in the pre-development process. That investment can't happen if there's uncertainty in the regulatory or the provincial government or any government environment.”

Gosal said he thinks success would include the government launching the housing roundtable and beginning work on the policies that “will make the biggest impact today.”

“And that priority will be set by not only the provincial government, but also the roundtable participants,” he said.

“The outcome [should] be: you would start to see movement in the housing sector, in the development sector, more activity, pre-sales actually starting to be sold, movement in the construction of housing.”

Success would also mean reducing enough costs to make housing more affordable to build, according to Drummond.

“When we get enough costs out of the system, [then] we can deliver a unit for the wages that people make in British Columbia,” he said.
